medical.title: How the brain keeps its options straight at decision time
medical.summary: A new study by neuroscientists at MIT's Picower Institute for Learning and Memory shows how the brain encodes information throughout the decision-making process to keep options clearly in mind and ensure that chosen and unchosen options are remembered.

medical.title: Are too many Americans taking antidepressants?
medical.summary: Drugs for treating depression are among the most prescribed categories of medications in the U.S.—1 in 6 American adults take them.

medical.title: Scientists uncover how cells surrounding primary liver tumors may help fuel cancer
medical.summary: UCLA researchers have identified a pathway in liver cells that may explain how statins could help prevent or slow the development of liver cancer associated with fatty liver disease.

medical.title: Rare variant reveals new hereditary retinal disease that can first impair night vision
medical.summary: An international team of researchers led by the University Hospital and University of Bonn, as well as the universities of Edinburgh, Basel and Pennsylvania, has identified a previously unrecognized form of inherited retinal degeneration caused by a specific variant in the EFEMP1 gene. The disease primarily affects the peripheral retina and the rod photoreceptors responsible for vision in dim light and darkness. Importantly, rod function may already be severely impaired while the retina still appears largely normal on clinical examination. The study results have now been published in the journal JAMA Ophthalmology.

medical.title: Stress hormone timing creates a different kind of obesity, study suggests
medical.summary: Obesity caused by disrupted stress-hormone rhythms is metabolically very different from obesity caused by a high-fat diet, according to a new preclinical study by Weill Cornell Medicine investigators. The researchers found in mice that glucocorticoid-rhythm disruption concentrates insulin resistance in skeletal muscle while preserving key insulin responses in fat tissue and liver. This allows fat tissue to continue storing lipids, while the liver remains largely protected from the fat accumulation typically seen with high-fat-diet obesity.

medical.title: 'Power naps' may improve clinical performance for sleep-deprived anesthesiology residents
medical.summary: For anesthesiology residents working 24-hour shifts, providing brief, scheduled "nap opportunities" may lead to better clinical performance, reports a clinical trial in the October 2026 issue of Anesthesiology.

medical.title: Neurosurveillance paradigm breaks imaging time barrier to reveal new clues about brain disease
medical.summary: Researchers at Johns Hopkins Medicine have demonstrated a new approach to brain imaging that enables continuous monitoring of brain activity and the physiologic changes associated with neurological disease progression for more than 24 hours in freely moving mouse models. The cloud-based miniaturized microscope, called CloudScope, operates autonomously and allows scientists to access live imaging data remotely from anywhere in the world, creating new opportunities to study diseases as they develop over time.

medical.title: Wireless brain-recording device enables animal neuroscience experiments in natural habitats
medical.summary: A new wireless device—lighter than a U.S. dime and shaped like a tiny chef's hat—can track the brain waves of animals as they move in natural habitats, opening doors to understanding complex behaviors that are impossible to study in the lab.

medical.title: Novel immunotherapy leads to complete regression of chemotherapy-resistant liver cancer in 3-year-old
medical.summary: A new report in the New England Journal of Medicine by researchers at Baylor College of Medicine, Texas Children's Hospital and Seattle Children's describes a complete regression of hepatoblastoma, the most common pediatric liver cancer, in a 3-year-old treated with a novel immunotherapy.

medical.title: When should patients see a rheumatologist for chronic back pain?
medical.summary: Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) is an inflammatory condition that causes chronic back pain and, if left untreated, can lead to fusion of the spinal or sacroiliac joints. The condition frequently remains underdiagnosed, with some studies suggesting that diagnosis can be delayed by up to 14 years. A new set of recommendations published in ACR Open Rheumatology aims to help improve the diagnosis of axSpA.

medical.title: Combination therapy may improve immune response against advanced prostate cancer
medical.summary: Combining the targeted therapy olaparib with an additional immunotherapy may improve immune response in a subgroup of patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer who responded poorly to initial treatment, according to a Northwestern Medicine study published in The Journal of Clinical Investigation.

science.title: Rare bird fossils from Bavaria reveal new species, including an eagle
science.summary: The Hammerschmiede clay pit near Pforzen in the eastern Allgäu is famous for its wealth of finds: Besides fossils of two early anthropoid apes, the remains of numerous vertebrate species have been uncovered in 11.6-million-year-old river sediments—but until now, very few birds.

science.title: Has gentle parenting gone too far?
science.summary: To be or not to be a gentle parent? That is the question. There is so much controversy these days about gentle parenting. What is it, and what is it not?

science.title: Q&A: The overlooked networks of heat resilience within communities
science.summary: As extreme heat becomes more frequent and severe, many people are turning to informal adaptation strategies—rigging up plastic sheeting overhead for shade, sharing water at a community tap and creating neighborhood cooling areas.

science.title: Under pressure: How a deep-sea protein adapts to an extreme environment
science.summary: Life in the deep sea is under immense pressure—literally. Such extreme conditions can disrupt the delicate structures of proteins essential to life. Yet somehow, the proteins in deep-sea creatures remain functional. This raises an intriguing question: how?

science.title: How to help your garden recover from a heat wave
science.summary: UK gardens took a battering this summer as a heat dome settled over western Europe, and much of the green and pleasant land turned a dusty beige.

science.title: Cell wall transport disruption exposes weakness in antibiotic-resistant bacteria
science.summary: Even highly antibiotic-resistant bacteria become more vulnerable when their cell wall transport system is disrupted, according to a new study from Umeå University. The discovery reveals a previously overlooked weakness that could help researchers develop new strategies to combat antibiotic resistance.

science.title: Psychologist wins Ig Nobel for proving rich drivers are the worst
science.summary: Paul K. Piff, UC Irvine associate professor of psychology, has officially been recognized for what millions of frustrated commuters have long suspected: The fancier the car, the worse the driver.

science.title: Fully recyclable hydrogel begins healing itself within minutes
science.summary: Imagine this. You pick up a contact lens from its container and—yikes!—it falls on the bathroom floor. Before you know it, your cat pounces, claws out. By the time you wrestle it back, the lens looks like a tiny chew toy. And then, just like that—the scratches fade away and the ripped edge seals itself up.

science.title: Learning without a brain—how bacteria store memories and remember the past like artificial neural networks
science.summary: Learning is often thought to require a brain. But learning is a broad concept that does not necessarily depend on neurons.

science.title: 'CRISPR-Combo' system speeds regeneration of hard-to-breed perennial crops
science.summary: Editing a plant's genes is only half the battle. Before a new, improved trait can ever reach a farmer's field, scientists must be able to grow a whole plant from just a few edited cells—a process that can be slow, unreliable and, for some plant species, impossible.

science.title: Portland report maps complex journeys through homelessness
science.summary: A new report from Portland State University's Homelessness Research and Action Collaborative (HRAC) and the OHSU-PSU School of Public Health offers an in-depth examination of how individuals navigate, survive and attempt to exit homelessness in Multnomah County. Titled "Without a Map: A Lived Experience Study of the Paths People Create Through Homelessness," the publication serves as the second and final part of the Pathways study.

science.title: NASA Invites Media to Djibouti Artemis Accords Signing Ceremony
science.summary: The Republic of Djibouti will sign the Artemis Accords during a ceremony at 11 a.m. EDT, Monday, Sept. 14, at NASA Headquarters in Washington, becoming the 72nd country signatory. NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson will host Ambassador of Djibouti to the United States Mohamed Siad Douale for the ceremony, together with U.S. State Department Assistant […]

environment.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
environment.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

environment.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
environment.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

environment.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

environment.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
environment.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.summary: As extreme heat becomes more frequent and severe, many people are turning to informal adaptation strategies—rigging up plastic sheeting overhead for shade, sharing water at a community tap and creating neighborhood cooling areas.

mix_items.title: Under pressure: How a deep-sea protein adapts to an extreme environment
mix_items.summary: Life in the deep sea is under immense pressure—literally. Such extreme conditions can disrupt the delicate structures of proteins essential to life. Yet somehow, the proteins in deep-sea creatures remain functional. This raises an intriguing question: how?

mix_items.title: How to help your garden recover from a heat wave
mix_items.summary: UK gardens took a battering this summer as a heat dome settled over western Europe, and much of the green and pleasant land turned a dusty beige.

mix_items.title: Cell wall transport disruption exposes weakness in antibiotic-resistant bacteria
mix_items.summary: Even highly antibiotic-resistant bacteria become more vulnerable when their cell wall transport system is disrupted, according to a new study from Umeå University. The discovery reveals a previously overlooked weakness that could help researchers develop new strategies to combat antibiotic resistance.

mix_items.title: Psychologist wins Ig Nobel for proving rich drivers are the worst
mix_items.summary: Paul K. Piff, UC Irvine associate professor of psychology, has officially been recognized for what millions of frustrated commuters have long suspected: The fancier the car, the worse the driver.

mix_items.title: Fully recyclable hydrogel begins healing itself within minutes
mix_items.summary: Imagine this. You pick up a contact lens from its container and—yikes!—it falls on the bathroom floor. Before you know it, your cat pounces, claws out. By the time you wrestle it back, the lens looks like a tiny chew toy. And then, just like that—the scratches fade away and the ripped edge seals itself up.

mix_items.title: Learning without a brain—how bacteria store memories and remember the past like artificial neural networks
mix_items.summary: Learning is often thought to require a brain. But learning is a broad concept that does not necessarily depend on neurons.

mix_items.title: 'CRISPR-Combo' system speeds regeneration of hard-to-breed perennial crops
mix_items.summary: Editing a plant's genes is only half the battle. Before a new, improved trait can ever reach a farmer's field, scientists must be able to grow a whole plant from just a few edited cells—a process that can be slow, unreliable and, for some plant species, impossible.

mix_items.title: Portland report maps complex journeys through homelessness
mix_items.summary: A new report from Portland State University's Homelessness Research and Action Collaborative (HRAC) and the OHSU-PSU School of Public Health offers an in-depth examination of how individuals navigate, survive and attempt to exit homelessness in Multnomah County. Titled "Without a Map: A Lived Experience Study of the Paths People Create Through Homelessness," the publication serves as the second and final part of the Pathways study.

mix_items.title: How the brain keeps its options straight at decision time
mix_items.summary: A new study by neuroscientists at MIT's Picower Institute for Learning and Memory shows how the brain encodes information throughout the decision-making process to keep options clearly in mind and ensure that chosen and unchosen options are remembered.

mix_items.title: Are too many Americans taking antidepressants?
mix_items.summary: Drugs for treating depression are among the most prescribed categories of medications in the U.S.—1 in 6 American adults take them.

mix_items.title: Scientists uncover how cells surrounding primary liver tumors may help fuel cancer
mix_items.summary: UCLA researchers have identified a pathway in liver cells that may explain how statins could help prevent or slow the development of liver cancer associated with fatty liver disease.

mix_items.title: Rare variant reveals new hereditary retinal disease that can first impair night vision
mix_items.summary: An international team of researchers led by the University Hospital and University of Bonn, as well as the universities of Edinburgh, Basel and Pennsylvania, has identified a previously unrecognized form of inherited retinal degeneration caused by a specific variant in the EFEMP1 gene. The disease primarily affects the peripheral retina and the rod photoreceptors responsible for vision in dim light and darkness. Importantly, rod function may already be severely impaired while the retina still appears largely normal on clinical examination. The study results have now been published in the journal JAMA Ophthalmology.

mix_items.title: Stress hormone timing creates a different kind of obesity, study suggests
mix_items.summary: Obesity caused by disrupted stress-hormone rhythms is metabolically very different from obesity caused by a high-fat diet, according to a new preclinical study by Weill Cornell Medicine investigators. The researchers found in mice that glucocorticoid-rhythm disruption concentrates insulin resistance in skeletal muscle while preserving key insulin responses in fat tissue and liver. This allows fat tissue to continue storing lipids, while the liver remains largely protected from the fat accumulation typically seen with high-fat-diet obesity.

mix_items.title: 'Power naps' may improve clinical performance for sleep-deprived anesthesiology residents
mix_items.summary: For anesthesiology residents working 24-hour shifts, providing brief, scheduled "nap opportunities" may lead to better clinical performance, reports a clinical trial in the October 2026 issue of Anesthesiology.

mix_items.title: Neurosurveillance paradigm breaks imaging time barrier to reveal new clues about brain disease
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Johns Hopkins Medicine have demonstrated a new approach to brain imaging that enables continuous monitoring of brain activity and the physiologic changes associated with neurological disease progression for more than 24 hours in freely moving mouse models. The cloud-based miniaturized microscope, called CloudScope, operates autonomously and allows scientists to access live imaging data remotely from anywhere in the world, creating new opportunities to study diseases as they develop over time.

mix_items.title: Wireless brain-recording device enables animal neuroscience experiments in natural habitats
mix_items.summary: A new wireless device—lighter than a U.S. dime and shaped like a tiny chef's hat—can track the brain waves of animals as they move in natural habitats, opening doors to understanding complex behaviors that are impossible to study in the lab.

mix_items.title: Novel immunotherapy leads to complete regression of chemotherapy-resistant liver cancer in 3-year-old
mix_items.summary: A new report in the New England Journal of Medicine by researchers at Baylor College of Medicine, Texas Children's Hospital and Seattle Children's describes a complete regression of hepatoblastoma, the most common pediatric liver cancer, in a 3-year-old treated with a novel immunotherapy.

mix_items.title: When should patients see a rheumatologist for chronic back pain?
mix_items.summary: Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) is an inflammatory condition that causes chronic back pain and, if left untreated, can lead to fusion of the spinal or sacroiliac joints. The condition frequently remains underdiagnosed, with some studies suggesting that diagnosis can be delayed by up to 14 years. A new set of recommendations published in ACR Open Rheumatology aims to help improve the diagnosis of axSpA.

mix_items.title: Combination therapy may improve immune response against advanced prostate cancer
mix_items.summary: Combining the targeted therapy olaparib with an additional immunotherapy may improve immune response in a subgroup of patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer who responded poorly to initial treatment, according to a Northwestern Medicine study published in The Journal of Clinical Investigation.

mix_items.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
mix_items.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

mix_items.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
mix_items.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

mix_items.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

mix_items.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
mix_items.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.
